text.p: Kentucky's two largest electric companies have agreed to merge, creating a company which would control 1.7 percent of the nation's generating capacity.
Officials told a news conference on Wednesday that they do not expect opposition to their proposal from state or federal regulators.

KU Energy Corp chief executive Michael Whitley said his company's planned merger into LG&E Energy Corp faces none of the georgraphic and transmission limits that led the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to reject the proposed merger of Northern States Power Co and Wisconsin Energy Corp .
Whitley said Kentucky officials informed of the merger plans Wednesday were "very, very supportive," adding, "We will be guaranteeing (our) customers a nearly two percent reduction in energy costs."
PaineWebber's Bert Kramer said the merged company "is not big enough to cause FERC problems."
In announcing the merger, the companies projected non-fuel savings of over $760 million over 10 years. They told analysts these savings would be shared 50-50 with customers.
Kramer said "the only question, did LG&E (agree to) pay too much" for KU.
The companies said KU holders would receive 1.67 shares of LG&E stock for each share now held in an exchange valued at $1.54 billion based on Tuesday's closing price of $24.38 per LG&E share.
LG&E chief executive Rober W. Hale told the news conference this would reduce LG&E's earnings per share $0.01 or $0.02 in the first year of operation as a merged company.
After that, the transaction is expected to be accretive to earnings, the company's announcement said.
First Call's consensus estimate shows LG&E earning $1.68 a share this year, up from $1.60 last year, and projects $1.79 a share for 1998.

Their utility operations -- Kentucky Utilities Co and Louisville Gas and Electric Co -- would continue as separate subsidiaries. Other utilities operating in Kentucky include American Electric Power Co Inc's Kentucky Power Co and CINergy Corp's Union Light, Heat & Power Co.

The combined holding companies will control 6,600 megawatts of generating capacity owned by the two utilities, 800 megawatts in non-utility power plants across the U.S., and the 2,500 megawatts of generation owned by the Ogletghorpe Cooperative and 1,700 megawatts controlled by the Big Rivers Cooperative.
Eighty percent of that power is coal fired, Hale said, adding the rest is from natural gas fired and hydro plants.
As recently as early this month, the two companies were competing for control of the Big Rivers power, which was also sought by PacifiCorp, Whitley said.
Hale said the bankruptcy court is expected to confirmation LG&E's control of Big Rivers' capacity on June 9.
In the future, he told reporters, the merged company expects to remain the nation's "third largest power marketer and continue to look for other acquisitions."
This "is a beginning for us, not an end," Hale concluded.
